questions.title: What is a class in Python?
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint or template used to create objects. It defines the attributes and methods that its instances can have.

questions.title: What is an object?
questions.answer: An object is an instance of a class. It has its own identity, state and behaviour.
questions.code:
class Student:
    pass

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
print(type(s1))  # <class '__main__.Student'>

questions.title: What is the difference between a class and an object?
questions.answer:
| Class                           | Object                       |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Blueprint                       | Instance of a class          |
| Defines structure and behaviour | Holds actual state           |
| Created using `class`           | Created by calling the class |
| Logical definition              | Runtime entity               |

questions.title: How do you create an object in Python?
questions.answer: We call the class as if it were a function.

questions.title: What is the purpose of self?
questions.answer: `self` refers to the current instance of the class. It allows instance methods to access or modify that object's attributes.

questions.title: Is self a Python keyword?
questions.answer: No. `self` is a naming convention, not a reserved keyword. We can use another name, but using `self` improves readability and follows Python conventions.

questions.title: What happens internally when we call an instance method?
questions.answer:
Python binds the instance to the method. When we call `obj.show()`, Python automatically passes the instance as the first argument.

Conceptually:
questions.code:
# When calling an instance method:
obj.show()

# Python translates it internally to:
ClassName.show(obj)

questions.title: What is an attribute?
questions.answer: An attribute is a value associated with an object or class. For example, an employee's name and salary can be attributes.

questions.title: What is an instance attribute?
questions.answer: An instance attribute belongs to a particular object. Different instances can hold different values.
questions.code:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

s1 = Student("Abhiraj")
s2 = Student("Rahul")
print(s1.name)
print(s2.name)

questions.title: What is a class attribute?
questions.answer: A class attribute is defined at the class level and is shared through the class unless an instance shadows it with its own attribute.
questions.code:
class Student:
    college = "SVCE"

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
print(s1.college)
print(s2.college)

questions.title: What is the difference between instance and class attributes?
questions.answer:
| Instance attribute           | Class attribute                    |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Associated with an instance  | Associated with a class            |
| Usually defined using `self` | Defined in the class body          |
| Can differ between instances | Shared unless shadowed             |
| Accessed through an instance | Accessed through class or instance |

questions.title: How can you dynamically add attributes to an object?
questions.answer: Python generally allows us to add attributes dynamically to instances.
questions.code:
class Student:
    pass

s = Student()
s.name = "Abhiraj"
s.age = 21
print(s.name)

questions.title: Can two objects of the same class have different attributes?
questions.answer: Yes. Unless the class restricts dynamic attributes, each object can have its own attributes.
questions.code:
class Student:
    pass

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
s1.name = "A"
s2.roll_no = 101

questions.title: What is object identity?
questions.answer: Object identity indicates whether two references point to the same object. We can inspect it using `id()` and compare identities using `is`.

questions.title: What is the difference between is and ==?
questions.answer: `is` checks whether two references point to the same object. `==` checks whether two objects are equal according to their equality implementation.
questions.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b)  # True (values equal)
print(a is b)  # False (different objects in memory)

questions.title: What is __dict__ in a Python object?
questions.answer: For ordinary instances that have an instance dictionary, `__dict__` stores their instance attributes as key-value pairs.

questions.title: Can a class have no methods?
questions.answer: Yes. A class can be used purely to represent data or as a marker type.
questions.code:
class Employee:
    pass

questions.title: What is the difference between type() and isinstance()?
questions.answer: `type()` returns the exact type of an object, whereas `isinstance()` checks whether an object is an instance of a class or any of its subclasses.
questions.code:
class Animal:
    pass

class Dog(Animal):
    pass

d = Dog()
print(type(d) == Animal)     # False
print(isinstance(d, Animal)) # True

questions.title: What is a constructor in Python?
questions.answer: A constructor is the object-creation mechanism associated with calling a class. In Python, `__new__()` creates and returns the object, while `__init__()` initializes the newly created instance.

questions.title: What is __init__()?
questions.answer: `__init__()` is an initializer method called after an instance has been created. It initializes the object's attributes.

questions.title: What is __new__()?
questions.answer: `__new__()` is responsible for creating and returning a new instance. It is a static method in behaviour and conventionally receives `cls` as its first argument.

questions.title: What is the difference between __new__() and __init__()?
questions.answer:
| `__new__()`                                               | `__init__()`                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Creates the instance                                      | Initializes the instance                |
| Receives `cls`                                            | Receives `self`                         |
| Must return an instance to continue normal initialization | Must return `None`                      |
| Runs before `__init__()`                                  | Runs after successful instance creation |

questions.title: In which order are __new__() and __init__() called?
questions.answer: First `__new__()` creates and returns the instance. Then Python invokes `__init__()` on that instance if it is an instance of the class being constructed.

questions.title: Can __init__() return a value?
questions.answer: No. It must return `None`. Returning another value explicitly causes a `TypeError`.

questions.title: Can __new__() return an object of another class?
questions.answer: Yes. But if it returns an object that isn't an instance of the class being constructed, Python doesn't call that class's `__init__()` through the normal construction process.

questions.title: Can we override __new__()?
questions.answer: Yes. We generally override it when controlling object creation, particularly for immutable types, singleton-like patterns or custom instance allocation.

questions.title: Why is __new__() important for immutable objects?
questions.answer: Immutable objects cannot have their value changed after creation. Therefore, when creating custom immutable objects, we may need to set their value inside `__new__()`.

questions.title: Is __init__() called every time we access an object?
questions.answer: No. It is called during normal instance construction, not every time we access an existing object.

questions.title: What happens if we don't define __init__()?
questions.answer: Python uses the inherited initializer if one is available, otherwise the default object initialization behaviour applies.

questions.title: Does Python support constructor overloading?
questions.answer: Python doesn't support traditional method overloading by defining multiple methods with the same name. We can achieve flexible construction using default arguments, `*args`, `kwargs` or alternative class methods.

questions.title: How do you create multiple ways to construct an object?
questions.answer: We can use class methods as alternative constructors.

questions.title: What is the difference between object.__new__() and object.__init__()?
questions.answer: `object.__new__()` is responsible for allocating a new instance, while `object.__init__()` performs the default initialization step, which generally does nothing.

questions.title: What happens if __new__() returns None?
questions.answer: Python won't call `__init__()` because the returned object isn't an instance of the class being constructed. The class call returns `None`.

questions.title: Can we create a singleton using __new__()?
questions.answer: Yes. We can cache the instance and return the same instance on subsequent calls. However, we must also consider repeated initialization and thread safety.

questions.title: What is the role of type.__call__() in object creation?
questions.answer:
When a class is called, its metaclass's `__call__()` controls the construction process. For a typical class using `type` as its metaclass, it coordinates `__new__()` and `__init__()`.

# Section 3: Instance Members (Questions 36–48)

questions.title: What are instance variables?
questions.answer: Instance variables are attributes associated with individual objects. Each instance can have its own values.

questions.title: What are instance methods?
questions.answer: Instance methods are methods that operate on a particular object. They receive the instance as the first argument, conventionally named `self`.

questions.title: How do you define an instance method?
questions.answer: An instance method is defined inside a class using `def` and takes `self` as its first parameter to represent the object instance calling the method. It can access and modify instance attributes via `self`.

questions.title: Can an instance method access class variables?
questions.answer: Yes. An instance method can access both instance attributes and class attributes.

questions.title: Can an instance method modify class variables?
questions.answer: Yes, but we need to access and reassign the class attribute through the class itself if we intend to modify shared class-level state.

questions.title: What happens if we assign a class variable using self?
questions.answer: It normally creates or updates an instance attribute, shadowing the class attribute rather than modifying the shared class variable.
questions.code:
class Student:
    college = "SVCE"

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
s1.college = "IIT"
print(s1.college)       # IIT (instance attribute)
print(s2.college)       # SVCE (class attribute)
print(Student.college)  # SVCE (class attribute)

questions.title: Can instance variables be created outside __init__()?
questions.answer: Yes. We can create them in any instance method or dynamically through an instance.

questions.title: What is the difference between instance state and class state?
questions.answer: Instance state contains data specific to an object. Class state contains data associated with the class and commonly shared across instances.

questions.title: What is self.__class__?
questions.answer: It refers to the actual class of the current instance.

questions.title: Can an instance method call another instance method?
questions.answer: Yes. We can call it using `self.method_name()`.

questions.title: Can we delete an instance attribute?
questions.answer: Yes. We use the `del` statement or `delattr()`.

questions.title: What happens when an instance attribute doesn't exist?
questions.answer: Python searches the class and its inheritance hierarchy after checking the instance's attribute storage. If it cannot find the attribute, it generally raises `AttributeError`.

questions.title: What is attribute lookup?
questions.answer:
Attribute lookup is the process Python follows to find an attribute on an object. It involves instance storage, class attributes, inheritance and potentially descriptor behaviour or custom attribute-access methods.

# Section 4: Class Members and Class Methods (Questions 49–63)

questions.title: What is a class variable?
questions.answer: A class variable is defined inside the class body but outside instance methods. It belongs to the class and is accessible through the class and its instances.

questions.title: What is a class method?
questions.answer: A class method is a method bound to the class rather than a particular instance. It receives the class as its first argument, conventionally named `cls`.

questions.title: Why do we use @classmethod?
questions.answer: We use class methods when an operation needs access to the class itself, such as updating class-level data or implementing alternative constructors.

questions.title: What is the difference between self and cls?
questions.answer:
| self                       | cls                     |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Refers to current instance | Refers to current class |
| Used in instance methods   | Used in class methods   |
| Accesses instance state    | Accesses class state    |

questions.title: Can a class method access instance variables?
questions.answer: Not directly because it doesn't receive a particular instance. However, it can access instance variables if an instance is explicitly passed to it.

questions.title: Can we call a class method using an object?
questions.answer: Yes. Python binds the class to the class method even when we access it through an instance.

questions.title: Can a class method create objects?
questions.answer: Yes. This is one of its common use cases.

questions.title: Why use cls() instead of hardcoding the class name?
questions.answer: Using `cls()` supports inheritance. If a subclass inherits the class method, the method can create an instance of that subclass instead of always creating the parent class.

questions.title: Can class variables be overridden by subclasses?
questions.answer: Yes. A subclass can define its own class attribute with the same name, which shadows the inherited attribute during lookup.

questions.title: What happens when we modify a class variable through a subclass?
questions.answer: Reassigning the attribute through the subclass creates or updates a binding on the subclass, rather than necessarily changing the parent class's binding.

questions.title: What is vars()?
questions.answer: `vars()` returns the `__dict__` attribute of an object when available. When called without an argument, it returns the current local namespace.

questions.title: What is the difference between vars() and dir()?
questions.answer: `vars()` generally exposes an object's attribute dictionary, while `dir()` provides a list of names available through the object, including inherited and dynamically available attributes.

questions.title: Can class methods be inherited?
questions.answer: Yes. Subclasses inherit class methods unless they override them.

questions.title: Can a class method call another class method?
questions.answer: Yes. We can use `cls.other_method()`.

questions.title: When would you use a class variable instead of an instance variable in a real project?
questions.answer:
I would use class variables for genuinely shared configuration or class-level metadata, such as a default category. For user-specific data, employee details or transaction state, I would use instance variables to avoid accidental state sharing.

# Section 5: Static Methods (Questions 64–76)

questions.title: What is a static method?
questions.answer: A static method is a method defined inside a class using `@staticmethod`. It doesn't automatically receive `self` or `cls`. It is useful for utility operations logically related to a class.

questions.title: What is the difference between instance, class and static methods?
questions.answer:
| Feature         | Instance method           | Class method           | Static method       |
| --------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------- |
| Decorator       | None                      | `@classmethod`         | `@staticmethod`     |
| First argument  | `self`                    | `cls`                  | None automatically  |
| Instance access | Yes                       | No automatic access    | No automatic access |
| Class access    | Possible through instance | Yes                    | Yes                 |
| Common use      | Instance behaviour        | Class-level operations | Utility operations  |

questions.title: Does a static method access class variables?
questions.answer: It can access class variables using the class name explicitly, but Python doesn't automatically pass the class to it.

questions.title: Can a static method access instance variables?
questions.answer: Not directly. It needs an instance to be explicitly passed as an argument.

questions.title: Can we call a static method using an object?
questions.answer: Yes. It can be called through either the class or an instance.

questions.title: Can static methods be inherited?
questions.answer: Yes. Static methods are inherited like other class attributes and methods.

questions.title: Why not define a utility function outside the class?
questions.answer: If the utility is closely related to the class's responsibility, keeping it inside the class improves organization. Otherwise, a standalone function is often simpler and more appropriate.

questions.title: Can a static method call an instance method?
questions.answer: Yes, but it must receive an instance explicitly and call the method through that instance.

questions.title: Is @staticmethod mandatory for methods without self?
questions.answer: No. But without it, accessing a normal function through an instance invokes descriptor binding and may automatically pass the instance, causing an argument mismatch.

questions.title: Can we use @staticmethod and @classmethod together?
questions.answer: They can be composed using descriptors, but this is uncommon and usually unnecessary. I would prefer a clear method design rather than combining them without a specific requirement.

questions.title: What is a descriptor in Python?
questions.answer: A descriptor is an object that defines one or more of `__get__()`, `__set__()` or `__delete__()`. Descriptors control attribute access. Properties, methods, static methods and class methods use descriptor behaviour.

questions.title: Why does a normal function behave differently inside and outside a class?
questions.answer: Functions implement the descriptor protocol. When accessed through an instance, a normal function becomes a bound method and receives the instance automatically.

questions.title: When would you choose a static method over a class method?
questions.answer:
When the operation doesn't need automatic access to either the instance or class. If I need subclass-aware construction or class-level state, I prefer a class method.

# Section 6: Encapsulation (Questions 77–94)

questions.title: What is encapsulation?
questions.answer: Encapsulation means grouping data and related behaviour inside a class while controlling how that data is accessed and modified. It helps protect object state and maintain valid data.

questions.title: What are the access modifiers in Python?
questions.answer:
Python conventionally uses three naming styles:

1. Public: `name`
2. Protected: `_name`
3. Private: `__name`

Unlike Java, Python doesn't enforce these access levels in the same way.

questions.title: What is a public attribute?
questions.answer: A public attribute can be accessed directly from inside and outside the class.

questions.title: What is a protected attribute?
questions.answer: A protected attribute starts with a single underscore. It indicates that the attribute is intended for internal use or subclass use, but this is only a convention.

questions.title: What is a private attribute?
questions.answer: An attribute beginning with two leading underscores is subject to name mangling. Python changes its internal name to reduce accidental name conflicts, particularly in inheritance.

questions.title: Does Python have truly private variables?
questions.answer: Python doesn't provide strict private instance variables like Java or C++. Double-underscore attributes undergo name mangling, but they can still be accessed using the mangled name.

questions.title: What is name mangling?
questions.answer: Name mangling is a mechanism where Python transforms an identifier beginning with at least two underscores and not ending with two underscores into a name containing the class name.

questions.title: Why does Python use name mangling?
questions.answer: Mainly to prevent accidental name collisions between parent and child classes. It is not intended as a security mechanism.

questions.title: What is the difference between _name and __name?
questions.answer:
| `_name`                   | `__name`                      |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Single leading underscore | Double leading underscores    |
| Internal-use convention   | Triggers name mangling        |
| Name remains unchanged    | Name is transformed           |
| No automatic protection   | Reduces inheritance conflicts |

questions.title: What is a property in Python?
questions.answer: A property allows us to access a method like an attribute. It helps implement controlled attribute access and validation.

questions.title: Why use @property instead of normal getter and setter methods?
questions.answer: Properties allow us to add validation or computed behaviour while preserving attribute-style access. They also let us change the internal implementation without changing the public interface.

questions.title: What is a setter?
questions.answer: A setter is a method decorated with `@property_name.setter`. It controls how a property's value is assigned.

questions.title: What is a deleter?
questions.answer: A deleter uses `@property_name.deleter` to define behaviour when a property is deleted using `del`.

questions.title: Can we make a read-only property?
questions.answer: Yes. We can define a property without providing a setter.

questions.title: What is data hiding?
questions.answer: Data hiding means restricting or discouraging direct access to internal object data and exposing controlled operations instead.

questions.title: Is encapsulation the same as abstraction?
questions.answer: No. Encapsulation groups data and behaviour and controls access. Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes essential functionality.

questions.title: How would you implement encapsulation in an Employee Management System?
questions.answer: I would keep employee salary and other sensitive business state behind controlled methods or properties. I would validate salary updates before changing the internal state.

questions.title: Does encapsulation guarantee security?
questions.answer:
No. Python's access conventions and name mangling are not security boundaries. Real security requires appropriate authorization, authentication and data-protection mechanisms.

# Section 7: Inheritance (Questions 95–119)

questions.title: What is inheritance?
questions.answer: Inheritance allows a child class to reuse and extend the attributes and methods of a parent class. It supports code reuse and hierarchical relationships.

questions.title: What is a parent class?
questions.answer: A parent class, also called a base or superclass, is the class whose functionality is inherited by another class.

questions.title: What is a child class?
questions.answer: A child class, also called a derived or subclass, inherits functionality from its parent class and can add or override behaviour.

questions.title: What are the different types of inheritance?
questions.answer:
1. Single inheritance.
2. Multiple inheritance.
3. Multilevel inheritance.
4. Hierarchical inheritance.
5. Hybrid inheritance.

questions.title: What is single inheritance?
questions.answer: A child class inherits from one parent class.

questions.title: What is multiple inheritance?
questions.answer: A child class inherits from more than one parent class.

questions.title: What is multilevel inheritance?
questions.answer: Multilevel inheritance occurs when a class inherits from another derived class, creating multiple levels of inheritance.

questions.title: What is hierarchical inheritance?
questions.answer: It occurs when multiple child classes inherit from the same parent class.

questions.title: What is hybrid inheritance?
questions.answer: Hybrid inheritance is a combination of two or more inheritance types, such as multiple and multilevel inheritance.

questions.title: Does Python support multiple inheritance?
questions.answer: Yes. Python supports multiple inheritance and uses the Method Resolution Order to determine which method is selected.

questions.title: What is method overriding?
questions.answer: Method overriding happens when a child class provides its own implementation of an inherited method with a compatible signature.

questions.title: Why do we use method overriding?
questions.answer: It allows subclasses to provide specialized behaviour while maintaining a common interface inherited from the parent class.

questions.title: What is the difference between method overriding and method overloading?
questions.answer:
| Overriding                       | Overloading                                                           |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Child redefines inherited method | Same operation supports different argument combinations               |
| Associated with inheritance      | Doesn't require inheritance                                           |
| Supported directly               | No traditional signature-based overloading                            |
| Runtime method dispatch          | Can be approximated using defaults, dispatch tools or argument checks |

questions.title: Does Python support method overloading?
questions.answer: Python doesn't support traditional method overloading based on different parameter signatures. Defining the same method name again replaces the earlier class-body binding.

questions.title: How can you achieve method overloading-like behaviour?
questions.answer: We can use default parameters, `*args`, `kwargs`, or `functools.singledispatch` for type-based function dispatch.

questions.title: What is the diamond problem?
questions.answer:
The diamond problem occurs when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor. Both parent classes may inherit the same method, creating ambiguity about which implementation should execute.

questions.title: How does Python solve the diamond problem?
questions.answer: Python uses Method Resolution Order and C3 linearization to establish a consistent order for searching classes.

questions.title: What is the difference between inheritance and composition?
questions.answer: Inheritance represents an IS-A relationship, whereas composition represents a HAS-A relationship. Inheritance reuses behaviour through a class hierarchy; composition builds functionality by combining objects.

questions.title: What is the IS-A relationship?
questions.answer: It represents inheritance. For example, a Dog IS-A Animal.

questions.title: What is the HAS-A relationship?
questions.answer: It represents an object containing or using another object. For example, a Car HAS-A Engine.

questions.title: Can a child class access private parent attributes?
questions.answer: It cannot access a double-underscore parent attribute directly using its original name because name mangling changes the identifier. The mangled attribute can still be accessed, but that is generally not recommended.

questions.title: Does a child class automatically call the parent constructor?
questions.answer: If the child doesn't define its own initializer, it inherits the parent's initializer. If it defines its own `__init__()`, the parent initializer isn't automatically called; we normally use `super().__init__()` when parent initialization is required.

questions.title: What happens when a child class doesn't override a parent method?
questions.answer: Python looks up the method through the inheritance hierarchy and uses the inherited implementation if it finds one.

questions.title: Can a child class override a class variable?
questions.answer: Yes. A child class can define a class attribute with the same name as a parent class attribute.

questions.title: What are the risks of deep inheritance hierarchies?
questions.answer:
They can create tight coupling, make debugging difficult, introduce fragile dependencies and make changes harder to understand. I prefer shallow inheritance and composition when appropriate.

# Section 8: Polymorphism (Questions 120–137)

questions.title: What is polymorphism?
questions.answer: Polymorphism means one interface can represent different implementations. Different objects can respond to the same method call according to their own behaviour.

questions.title: What are the types of polymorphism?
questions.answer:
Commonly discussed forms include:

- Compile-time polymorphism, such as traditional method overloading.
- Runtime polymorphism, such as method overriding and dynamic dispatch.
- Parametric polymorphism, such as generic programming.
- Ad-hoc polymorphism, such as operator overloading.

Python's dynamic model supports several of these ideas, but not every language implements them identically.

questions.title: What is runtime polymorphism?
questions.answer: Runtime polymorphism occurs when the implementation selected for a method call depends on the actual object at runtime.

questions.title: What is duck typing?
questions.answer:
Duck typing means that Python focuses on what an object can do rather than requiring it to belong to a particular class.

"If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, treat it like a duck."

questions.title: Does duck typing require inheritance?
questions.answer: No. Objects don't need a common parent class. They only need to provide the required behaviour.

questions.title: What is dynamic method dispatch?
questions.answer: Dynamic method dispatch is the process of selecting the appropriate overridden method based on the actual object's type at runtime.

questions.title: What is operator overloading?
questions.answer: Operator overloading allows us to define how operators behave for custom objects using special methods.

questions.title: What is the difference between overriding and overloading in Python?
questions.answer: Overriding replaces inherited behaviour in a subclass. Traditional signature-based overloading isn't built into Python, although we can simulate it.

questions.title: Can Python achieve polymorphism without inheritance?
questions.answer: Yes. Duck typing allows unrelated classes to support the same interface and work with the same function.

questions.title: What is polymorphism through function arguments?
questions.answer: It means writing a function that accepts different objects and calls a common method or operation on them.

questions.title: How does Python handle polymorphism with built-in functions?
questions.answer: Many built-in functions operate on different types through their protocols. For example, `len()` works with strings, lists, tuples and custom objects implementing `__len__()`.

questions.title: What is structural typing?
questions.answer: Structural typing checks whether an object provides the required structure or operations rather than relying only on its declared inheritance. Python's `Protocol` system supports structural subtyping for static type checking.

questions.title: What is nominal typing?
questions.answer: Nominal typing determines compatibility based on explicitly declared type relationships, such as inheritance or implementation of a named interface.

questions.title: What is the difference between duck typing and polymorphism?
questions.answer: Polymorphism is the broader concept of using a common interface with different implementations. Duck typing is one way Python achieves polymorphic behaviour without requiring explicit inheritance.

questions.title: Can constructors be polymorphic?
questions.answer: Constructor behaviour can vary through overriding `__new__()` and `__init__()` in subclasses. Alternative class methods can also provide different construction behaviours.

questions.title: How is polymorphism useful in payment systems?
questions.answer: I can define a common payment interface and implement different payment providers such as UPI, cards and wallets. A payment service can call the same method without needing to know the internal implementation of each provider.

questions.title: What is Liskov Substitution Principle?
questions.answer: It states that objects of a subclass should be usable wherever objects of the parent class are expected without breaking the correctness of the program.

questions.title: What problems can poor polymorphic design create?
questions.answer:
It can cause unexpected behaviour, violated interface contracts, excessive conditional checks and subclasses that cannot safely replace their parent classes.

# Section 9: Abstraction (Questions 138–153)

questions.title: What is abstraction?
questions.answer: Abstraction means exposing essential functionality while hiding unnecessary implementation details. It helps users interact with a clear interface without understanding internal complexity.

questions.title: How do we implement abstraction in Python?
questions.answer: Python provides the `abc` module, which supports abstract base classes and abstract methods.

questions.title: What is an abstract class?
questions.answer: An abstract class is a class intended to provide a common interface or partial implementation. An abstract base class containing abstract methods cannot normally be instantiated until its abstract methods are implemented.

questions.title: What is an abstract method?
questions.answer: An abstract method is a method declared using `@abstractmethod`. Concrete subclasses must implement it before they can be instantiated.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the ABC module?
questions.answer: It provides infrastructure for defining abstract base classes and enforcing required methods during instantiation.

questions.title: Can an abstract class contain normal methods?
questions.answer: Yes. An abstract class can contain both abstract methods and fully implemented methods.

questions.title: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
questions.answer: Yes. An abstract class can define `__init__()` to initialize common state for subclasses.

questions.title: Can an abstract class have class methods and static methods?
questions.answer: Yes. Abstract base classes can define both. The `@abstractmethod` decorator can also be combined with supported method descriptors in the appropriate decorator order.

questions.title: Can we create an object of an abstract class?
questions.answer: Not if it still has unresolved abstract methods. Python raises a `TypeError` when we attempt to instantiate it.

questions.title: What happens if a subclass doesn't implement all abstract methods?
questions.answer: It remains abstract and cannot be instantiated until all abstract methods are implemented.

questions.title: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation?
questions.answer:
| Abstraction                     | Encapsulation                                |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Hides implementation complexity | Groups data and behaviour                    |
| Focuses on what an object does  | Focuses on controlling object state          |
| Often uses ABC and interfaces   | Often uses properties and naming conventions |
| Defines a contract              | Controls access and modification             |

questions.title: Does Python have interfaces?
questions.answer: Python doesn't have a separate interface keyword like Java. We can achieve similar behaviour through abstract base classes and structural typing using `Protocol`.

questions.title: What is Protocol in Python?
questions.answer: `Protocol` from the `typing` module supports structural subtyping. It allows us to define expected operations without requiring explicit inheritance.

questions.title: What is the difference between ABC and Protocol?
questions.answer: ABC supports explicit inheritance-based contracts and can enforce abstract methods at instantiation. Protocol primarily supports structural typing and static type checking without requiring explicit inheritance.

questions.title: What is the purpose of @abstractmethod?
questions.answer: It marks a method as abstract so that concrete subclasses must provide an implementation before they can be instantiated.

questions.title: When would you use abstraction in a backend application?
questions.answer:
For example, I could define a repository interface with methods such as `save()`, `find_by_id()` and `delete()`. PostgreSQL and other database implementations could then follow the same contract.

# Section 10: MRO, C3 Linearization and `super()` (Questions 154–177)

This is one of the hardest Python OOP interview areas. Make sure you understand the diamond problem and cooperative inheritance.

questions.title: What is MRO?
questions.answer: MRO stands for Method Resolution Order. It defines the order in which Python searches classes to find a method or attribute, especially when multiple inheritance is involved.

questions.title: How can you inspect MRO?
questions.answer: We can use the `mro()` method or the `__mro__` attribute.

questions.title: What is C3 linearization?
questions.answer: C3 linearization is the algorithm Python uses to calculate a consistent MRO. It preserves local precedence ordering and monotonicity while respecting the inheritance hierarchy.

questions.title: What is monotonicity in MRO?
questions.answer: Monotonicity means that the relative ordering of parent classes established in a base class's MRO should remain consistent when that class is inherited by another class.

questions.title: What are the rules of C3 linearization?
questions.answer:
The important principles are:

1. A class appears before its parent classes.
2. The declared order of direct parents is respected.
3. The relative order established by parent MROs is preserved.
4. Each class appears only once.

questions.title: Explain MRO with multiple inheritance.
questions.answer: In multiple inheritance, Python resolves methods using C3 Linearization (MRO). Here, `D` searches `B` first before `C` and `A`. Therefore, `d.show()` invokes `B.show()`, outputting `B`, and the MRO list shows `['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']`.

questions.title: What is super()?
questions.answer: `super()` provides a proxy that delegates attribute lookup to the next class in the MRO. It is commonly used to call inherited methods cooperatively.

questions.title: Does super() always call the parent class?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. It calls the next implementation in the MRO, which may be a sibling class in multiple inheritance rather than the direct parent.

questions.title: What is the difference between super() and directly calling the parent class?
questions.answer:
| `super()`                                 | Direct parent call                                      |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Follows MRO                               | Explicitly targets a named class                        |
| Supports cooperative multiple inheritance | Can bypass other classes in MRO                         |
| More flexible                             | Can create duplicate calls                              |
| Recommended for cooperative inheritance   | Useful only when explicit direct invocation is intended |

questions.title: How does super() work internally?
questions.answer: It creates a proxy object that performs attribute lookup starting after the specified class in the relevant MRO. In the common zero-argument form, Python determines the current class and instance or class context automatically.

questions.title: What is zero-argument super()?
questions.answer: It is the form `super()` that Python supports inside methods, allowing us to access the next implementation without explicitly specifying the current class and instance.

questions.title: Can super() be used in multiple inheritance?
questions.answer: Yes. It is especially important in multiple inheritance because it enables cooperative method calls following the MRO.

questions.title: What is cooperative multiple inheritance?
questions.answer: It is a design where classes consistently use `super()` to delegate method calls along the MRO so that each participating class can contribute to the operation.

questions.title: Predict the output.
questions.answer: The MRO is `D → B → C → A → object`. When `D().show()` is invoked, execution starts at `B.show()` which prints `B` and calls `super().show()`, moving to `C.show()` which prints `C` and calls `super().show()`, which moves to `A.show()` printing `A`.

questions.title: What happens if we directly call a parent method instead of using super()?
questions.answer: We may bypass classes that appear between the current class and the intended parent in the MRO. This can cause duplicated execution or skipped functionality.

questions.title: Can MRO produce an inconsistent hierarchy?
questions.answer: Yes. If the declared inheritance order conflicts with the ordering constraints of the base classes, Python raises a `TypeError` when creating the class.

questions.title: What is an inconsistent MRO example?
questions.answer: An inconsistent MRO occurs when Python's C3 Linearization cannot establish a monotonic hierarchy that respects the local precedence order of all parent classes. Inheriting from `A(X, Y)` and `B(Y, X)` introduces a cyclic conflict between `X` and `Y`, resulting in `TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO)`.
questions.code:
# Example of MRO inconsistency:
class X: pass
class Y: pass
class A(X, Y): pass
class B(Y, X): pass

# Inheriting from both A and B creates conflicting orders:
# class C(A, B): pass
# TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO)

questions.title: What is the role of object in MRO?
questions.answer: In Python 3, ordinary classes implicitly inherit from `object` if no other base class is specified. It is the root of the standard class hierarchy.

questions.title: What is the difference between old-style and new-style classes?
questions.answer: Old-style classes existed in Python 2. New-style classes were introduced in Python 2.2 and became the standard in Python 3. Python 3 classes use the new-style object model and C3 MRO.

questions.title: Can super() be used inside __init__()?
questions.answer: Yes. It is commonly used to initialize parent or cooperative base-class state.

questions.title: What happens when multiple parent classes have the same method?
questions.answer: Python chooses the first matching implementation according to the class's MRO.

questions.title: Does MRO apply only to methods?
questions.answer: No. MRO also affects ordinary attribute lookup across the class hierarchy.

questions.title: What is super(CurrentClass, self)?
questions.answer: It is the explicit form of `super()`. It returns a proxy that starts searching after `CurrentClass` in the MRO associated with `self`.

questions.title: Why is super() important in framework development?
questions.answer:
Frameworks often use inheritance and mixins. Cooperative `super()` calls allow different classes to contribute functionality without tightly coupling them to a particular parent class.

# Section 11: Composition (Questions 178–191)

questions.title: What is composition?
questions.answer: Composition is a design relationship where one object contains and uses another object to provide functionality. It represents a HAS-A relationship.

questions.title: What is a HAS-A relationship?
questions.answer: It means one object contains or uses another object. A Car HAS-A Engine.

questions.title: What is the difference between composition and inheritance?
questions.answer:
| Composition                       | Inheritance                |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| HAS-A relationship                | IS-A relationship          |
| Uses other objects                | Extends a parent class     |
| More flexible object combinations | Reuses inherited behaviour |
| Often reduces tight coupling      | Can create tight coupling  |

questions.title: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
questions.answer: Composition allows us to change dependencies more easily, reuse independent components and avoid deep inheritance hierarchies. It also makes testing easier when dependencies can be replaced.

questions.title: Give a real-world example of composition.
questions.answer: An Employee Management System can have an Employee object containing an Address object, Department object and ContactDetails object.

questions.title: Can a composed object be replaced at runtime?
questions.answer: Yes. If we design the containing class to depend on an interface or expected behaviour, we can replace its dependency with another implementation.

questions.title: What is dependency injection?
questions.answer: Dependency injection means providing an object's dependencies from outside rather than creating all dependencies internally.

questions.title: What is the difference between composition and dependency injection?
questions.answer: Composition describes how objects are combined. Dependency injection describes how those dependencies are supplied. They are related but different concepts.

questions.title: What is tight coupling?
questions.answer: Tight coupling occurs when one component depends heavily on the internal implementation of another component, making independent changes and testing difficult.

questions.title: What is loose coupling?
questions.answer: Loose coupling means components depend on stable interfaces or contracts rather than specific implementations.

questions.title: How would you use composition in a payment system?
questions.answer: I could create a PaymentService that receives a payment gateway dependency. Different gateway implementations could be supplied without changing the payment service's business logic.

questions.title: Can composition help with unit testing?
questions.answer: Yes. We can inject mock or fake dependencies to test one component independently of databases, APIs or external services.

questions.title: What is delegation in OOP?
questions.answer: Delegation occurs when an object forwards a responsibility or operation to another object that performs the actual work.

questions.title: Is composition always better than inheritance?
questions.answer:
No. Inheritance is appropriate when there is a genuine IS-A relationship and substitutability is maintained. Composition is preferable when we want to combine independent behaviours without creating a rigid hierarchy.

# Section 12: Aggregation (Questions 192–204)

questions.title: What is aggregation?
questions.answer: Aggregation is a HAS-A relationship in which one object uses or references another object, but the contained object can exist independently of the container.

questions.title: Give a real-world example of aggregation.
questions.answer: A Department has Employees. If the Department is deleted, the Employee objects can still exist independently.

questions.title: What is the difference between composition and aggregation?
questions.answer:
| Composition                                       | Aggregation                            |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Strong ownership relationship                     | Weaker ownership relationship          |
| Component is conceptually part of the owner       | Referenced object exists independently |
| Often shares lifecycle                            | Lifecycle is independent               |
| Example: Car and its Engine in a simplified model | Example: Department and Employee       |

Important: Python doesn't enforce these relationships at the language level. They are object-design concepts.

questions.title: Can an aggregated object exist without its container?
questions.answer: Yes. Aggregation means the referenced object has an independent lifecycle.

questions.title: Can multiple objects reference the same aggregated object?
questions.answer: Yes. Multiple containers can reference the same independently existing object.

questions.title: Does aggregation require a special Python keyword?
questions.answer: No. It is implemented using ordinary object references and appropriate class design.

questions.title: What is object ownership?
questions.answer: Object ownership describes which component is responsible for managing another object's lifecycle or responsibility. Python uses references and garbage collection rather than enforcing ownership rules like some languages.

questions.title: What is the difference between aggregation and association?
questions.answer: Association is a general relationship between objects. Aggregation is a more specific HAS-A association with weak ownership.

questions.title: What is association in OOP?
questions.answer: Association means two objects are related and interact with each other without necessarily owning one another.

questions.title: Can aggregation be implemented using dependency injection?
questions.answer: Yes. An object can receive an independently managed object through its constructor and retain a reference to it.

questions.title: What is a lifecycle dependency?
questions.answer: A lifecycle dependency exists when the existence of one component is conceptually tied to another component. Composition commonly models stronger lifecycle dependency than aggregation.

questions.title: How would you model Student and College?
questions.answer: A Student can be associated with a College, but the Student can conceptually exist independently of a particular College. I would model this as an association or aggregation depending on the business rules.

questions.title: Does deleting a Python reference automatically destroy an object?
questions.answer:
No. It removes that reference. The object remains alive as long as references or other lifetime mechanisms keep it alive. When it becomes unreachable, it becomes eligible for garbage collection.

# Section 13: Operator Overloading and Magic Methods (Questions 205–232)

This section is extremely important for Python interviews. You should know what happens internally when we use operators or built-in functions on custom objects.

questions.title: What are magic methods?
questions.answer:
Magic methods, also called special methods, are methods with double underscores that allow custom objects to integrate with Python's language features and protocols.

Examples include `__init__()`, `__str__()`, `__add__()` and `__len__()`.

questions.title: What is operator overloading?
questions.answer: Operator overloading means defining custom behaviour for operators such as `+`, `-`, `==` and `*` using special methods.

questions.title: How does the + operator work internally?
questions.answer: For custom objects, Python generally tries the left operand's `__add__()` method and may try the right operand's `__radd__()` if appropriate. If the operation isn't supported, it can raise a `TypeError`.

questions.title: What is __add__()?
questions.answer: `__add__()` defines the behaviour of the `+` operator for a custom object.

questions.title: What is __radd__()?
questions.answer: `__radd__()` is the reflected addition method. It allows an object to handle addition when it appears on the right side of the operator and the left operand doesn't handle the operation appropriately.

questions.title: What is __iadd__()?
questions.answer: It implements in-place addition, used by `+=`. If it isn't available or returns `NotImplemented`, Python can fall back to ordinary addition and assignment behaviour.

questions.title: What is the difference between __add__() and __iadd__()?
questions.answer: `__add__()` defines ordinary addition and generally produces a result. `__iadd__()` defines in-place addition and may mutate the existing object.

questions.title: What is __str__()?
questions.answer: `__str__()` defines the human-readable string representation of an object. It is used by `str()` and normally by `print()`.

questions.title: What is __repr__()?
questions.answer: `__repr__()` defines the developer-oriented representation of an object. Ideally, it should be unambiguous and, when practical, provide information useful for recreating the object.

questions.title: What is the difference between __str__() and __repr__()?
questions.answer:
| `__str__()`                   | `__repr__()`                       |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Human-readable representation | Developer-oriented representation  |
| Used by `str()`               | Used by `repr()`                   |
| Used by `print()` by default  | Used by interactive inspection     |
| Focuses on readability        | Focuses on clarity and unambiguity |

questions.title: What happens if we don't implement __str__()?
questions.answer: Python falls back to the object's `__repr__()` implementation when available. Otherwise, it uses the default object representation.

questions.title: What is __len__()?
questions.answer: It defines the behaviour of the built-in `len()` function for custom objects.

questions.title: What must __len__() return?
questions.answer: It must return a non-negative integer. Returning an invalid value causes an error.

questions.title: What is __eq__()?
questions.answer: It defines equality comparison using the `==` operator.

questions.title: What is NotImplemented?
questions.answer: `NotImplemented` is a special value that a binary operation method can return when it doesn't support the supplied operand types. It allows Python to try alternative dispatch mechanisms.

questions.title: What is __hash__()?
questions.answer: It returns an integer hash value used by hash-based collections such as sets and dictionaries.

questions.title: What is the relationship between __eq__() and __hash__()?
questions.answer: If two objects compare equal, they must have equal hash values. However, equal hash values don't guarantee equal objects.

questions.title: What happens if we override __eq__() without defining __hash__()?
questions.answer: Python normally sets `__hash__` to `None` when a class overrides `__eq__()` without defining a compatible hash implementation. Such instances become unhashable.

questions.title: Can mutable objects be dictionary keys?
questions.answer: They can be keys only if they are hashable and their hash and equality behaviour remain stable while used as keys. Mutable objects are generally not suitable dictionary keys.

questions.title: What is __call__()?
questions.answer: `__call__()` makes an object callable, allowing us to use the object like a function.

questions.title: What is __iter__()?
questions.answer: `__iter__()` returns an iterator for an object. It is used when we call `iter()` or start iterating through a `for` loop.

questions.title: What is __next__()?
questions.answer: `__next__()` returns the next item from an iterator. When there are no more items, it raises `StopIteration`.

questions.title: What is the difference between iterable and iterator?
questions.answer:
| Iterable                    | Iterator                                 |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Can provide an iterator     | Produces values one at a time            |
| Implements `__iter__()`     | Implements `__iter__()` and `__next__()` |
| Example: list, tuple        | Example: `iter(list)`                    |
| May be traversed repeatedly | Usually consumed during iteration        |

questions.title: How do you implement a custom iterator?
questions.answer: A custom iterator in Python implements `__iter__()` (which returns the iterator object, typically `self`) and `__next__()` (which yields the next element or raises `StopIteration` when the sequence ends).

questions.title: What is __enter__()?
questions.answer: `__enter__()` defines the setup behaviour when an object is used in a `with` statement. Its return value is assigned to the variable after `as`, if present.

questions.title: What is __exit__()?
questions.answer: `__exit__()` defines cleanup behaviour when execution leaves a `with` block. It receives exception information if an exception occurred.

questions.title: How do context managers use __enter__() and __exit__()?
questions.answer: Context managers implement the `__enter__()` and `__exit__()` magic methods. `__enter__()` sets up the resource and returns the bound target, while `__exit__()` executes deterministic teardown (closing files, releasing locks, terminating connections) even if exceptions occur.

questions.title: What does returning True from __exit__() mean?
questions.answer:
If an exception occurred inside the `with` block, returning a truthy value from `__exit__()` suppresses that exception. Returning a false value allows it to propagate.

# Section 14: Object Lifecycle and Memory Management (Questions 233–243)

questions.title: What is the object lifecycle in Python?
questions.answer: An object's lifecycle generally includes creation, initialization, usage and eventual cleanup. Python manages object memory automatically through reference counting and garbage collection in CPython.

questions.title: What is __del__()?
questions.answer: `__del__()` is a finalizer method that Python may invoke when an object is about to be finalized.

questions.title: Is del the same as __del__()?
questions.answer: No. `del` is a Python statement that removes a reference or deletes a name or attribute. `__del__()` is a special method that may be invoked during object finalization.

questions.title: Does del object immediately destroy the object?
questions.answer: No. It removes that reference. The object may remain alive if other references still point to it.
questions.code:
class Student:
    pass

s1 = Student()
s2 = s1
del s1
print(s2)  # Object still exists; reference count decreased from 2 to 1

questions.title: What is reference counting?
questions.answer: Reference counting is a memory-management technique in which Python tracks references to objects. In CPython, when an object's reference count reaches zero, it can generally be deallocated immediately.

questions.title: What is garbage collection?
questions.answer: Garbage collection is the process of reclaiming memory from objects that are no longer needed. Python includes a cyclic garbage collector to detect unreachable reference cycles.

questions.title: What is a reference cycle?
questions.answer: A reference cycle occurs when objects reference each other, directly or indirectly, preventing their reference counts from reaching zero even though they may be unreachable from the program.
questions.code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
b = A()
a.other = b
b.other = a

# Creating cyclic reference:
del a
del b

questions.title: What is the gc module?
questions.answer: The `gc` module provides interfaces for inspecting and controlling Python's cyclic garbage collector.
questions.code:
import gc

print(gc.isenabled())
print(gc.get_count())
gc.collect()

questions.title: What is the difference between __del__() and context managers?
questions.answer: `__del__()` is associated with object finalization, which isn't suitable for guaranteeing timely cleanup. Context managers provide a predictable cleanup mechanism when execution exits a `with` block.

questions.title: Why should we avoid depending on __del__() for resource cleanup?
questions.answer: Its execution timing isn't guaranteed, reference cycles can complicate finalization, and interpreter shutdown can create additional problems. I prefer context managers for files, database connections and locks.

questions.title: What is weak referencing in Python?
questions.answer: Weak references allow us to refer to an object without increasing its strong reference count. They are useful for caches and relationships where we don't want the reference itself to keep an object alive.
questions.code:
import weakref

class Student:
    pass

s = Student()
ref = weakref.ref(s)
print(ref() is s)  # True

del s
print(ref())        # None, once object is garbage collected

questions.title: Predict the output: Class variable or instance variable?
questions.answer: Assigning through `s1.college = "IIT"` creates an instance attribute on `s1` that shadows the class attribute. `Student.college` and `s2.college` continue reading the class attribute `SVCE`.
questions.code:
class Student:
    college = "SVCE"

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
s1.college = "IIT"
print(Student.college)
print(s1.college)
print(s2.college)

questions.title: Predict the output: Shared mutable class variable.
questions.answer: Both instances share the same class-level mutable list `subjects`. Mutating it through `s1` affects what `s2` observes.
questions.code:
class Student:
    subjects = []

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
s1.subjects.append("Python")
print(s2.subjects)

questions.title: Predict the output: Constructor inheritance.
questions.answer: The child class `B` defines its own `__init__()` method and overrides the parent constructor. Because it does not explicitly call `super().__init__()`, only `B` runs.

questions.title: Predict the output: Using super().
questions.answer: `B.__init__()` calls `super().__init__()`, executing `A.__init__()` first (printing `A`), and then prints `B`.

questions.title: Predict the output: Method overriding.
questions.answer: Method overriding: `C` overrides `show()`. Looking up `show()` on an instance of `C` resolves to `C.show`, printing `C`.

questions.title: Predict the output: Static method binding.
questions.answer: Static methods do not receive an automatic instance or class parameter. They can be invoked identically through either the instance `obj.show()` or class `A.show()` without difference.

questions.title: Predict the output: Class method inheritance.
questions.answer: The class method receives the class object through which it was called. When called via `A.show()`, `cls` is `A`. When called via `B.show()`, `cls` is `B`.

questions.title: Predict the output: Name mangling.
questions.answer: Due to Python's name mangling, attributes prefixed with double underscores (`__value`) are rewritten internally to `_ClassName__attributeName` (`_A__value`).

questions.title: Predict the output: Inheritance and name mangling.
questions.answer: AttributeError. The parent attribute is mangled to `_A__value`. In class `B`, the reference `self.__value` is mangled to `_B__value`, which does not exist.

questions.title: Predict the output: __str__() and __repr__().
questions.answer: `str(s)` explicitly invokes the user-facing `__str__()` method, while `repr(s)` invokes the formal representation `__repr__()` method.

questions.title: Predict the output: Equality versus identity.
questions.answer: Without an explicit `__eq__()` implementation, user-defined classes fall back to `is` (identity) equality. Since `a` and `b` are two distinct objects at different memory addresses, both `==` and `is` return `False`.
questions.code:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, roll):
        self.roll = roll

a = Student(101)
b = Student(101)
print(a == b)
print(a is b)

questions.title: Predict the output: Operator overloading.
questions.answer: The `+` operator invokes `__add__()`, creating and returning `Number(30)`. When `print()` formats the object, `__str__()` returns string `"30"`.

questions.title: Predict the output: __call__().
questions.answer: Implementing `__call__()` makes instances callable like functions. `callable(obj)` returns `True`, and `obj(10)` passes `10` to `__call__`, returning `20`.

questions.title: Predict the output: MRO.
questions.answer: MRO follows C3 linearization: `[D, B, C, A, object]`. Method lookup stops at the first match in the MRO, which is `B.show()`.

questions.title: Predict the output: super() in multiple inheritance.
questions.answer: In multiple inheritance with cooperative `super()`, calls traverse the complete MRO (`D -> B -> C -> A`). Each class prints its letter and forwards execution up the chain.

questions.title: Predict the output: Object identity.
questions.answer: `b = a` copies the object reference, so `a` and `b` point to the exact same object in memory (`True`). `c = Student()` creates a distinct new instance (`False`).
questions.code:
class Student:
    pass

a = Student()
b = a
c = Student()
print(a is b)
print(a is c)

questions.title: Predict the output: __new__() and __init__().
questions.answer: Python first allocates and creates the object through `__new__()` (printing `New`), and once the instance is returned, Python automatically calls `__init__()` on it (printing `Init`).

questions.title: How would you design an Employee Management System using OOP?
questions.answer: I would create separate classes for Employee, Department and Address. Employee would contain employee-specific information, while Department and Address would represent related objects. I would use composition where appropriate and keep business logic inside suitable service classes.

questions.title: How would you design a payment system using polymorphism?
questions.answer: I would define a common payment contract and implement separate classes for UPI, card and wallet payments. Each class would provide its own payment implementation. The payment service would work with the common contract rather than depending on specific implementations.

questions.title: How would you design a notification system using abstraction?
questions.answer: I would define a notification interface with a `send()` operation. EmailNotification, SMSNotification and PushNotification would implement that operation. This allows the application to use different notification providers without changing its core business logic.

questions.title: How would you prevent direct modification of an employee's salary?
questions.answer: I would use a property with a setter to validate salary updates and expose only the required operations. In a real backend, I would additionally enforce authorization in the service layer.

questions.title: How would you implement a reusable database connection manager?
questions.answer: I would separate connection management from business logic, expose a clear interface and inject the connection or session into repository classes. A context manager can ensure proper resource cleanup.

questions.title: How would you design a logging system using OOP?
questions.answer: I would define a logger interface or common contract and provide implementations for console, file and remote logging. This supports extensibility without changing the code that generates log messages.

questions.title: How would you decide between inheritance and composition?
questions.answer: I would first check whether the relationship represents a genuine IS-A relationship. If the requirement is simply to reuse or combine behaviour, I would generally consider composition. I would also consider substitutability, coupling and future changes.

questions.title: What is the SOLID principle?
questions.answer:
SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help create maintainable, extensible and loosely coupled software.

| Principle | Meaning                         |
| --------- | ------------------------------- |
| S         | Single Responsibility Principle |
| O         | Open/Closed Principle           |
| L         | Liskov Substitution Principle   |
| I         | Interface Segregation Principle |
| D         | Dependency Inversion Principle  |

questions.title: Explain Single Responsibility Principle.
questions.answer: A class should have one primary responsibility and one main reason to change. For example, an Employee class should represent employee-related behaviour rather than also managing database connections and sending emails.

questions.title: Explain Open/Closed Principle.
questions.answer: Software components should be open for extension but closed for modification. We should be able to add new behaviour without repeatedly changing stable existing code.

questions.title: Explain Liskov Substitution Principle.
questions.answer: A subclass should be usable wherever its parent class is expected without breaking the expected behaviour or contract.

questions.title: Explain Interface Segregation Principle.
questions.answer: A class shouldn't be forced to depend on methods it doesn't need. We should prefer smaller, focused interfaces instead of one large interface.

questions.title: Explain Dependency Inversion Principle.
questions.answer: High-level business logic should depend on abstractions rather than concrete low-level implementations. This helps us replace dependencies and test components independently.

questions.title: What is the difference between an OOP model and an ORM?
questions.answer: OOP models objects and their behaviour in an application. An ORM maps application objects to relational database tables and helps interact with the database using object-oriented abstractions.

questions.title: How do OOP concepts help in FastAPI backend development?
questions.answer: I can use classes to organize services, repositories and business entities. Dependency injection can provide database sessions and services, ABC or Protocol can define contracts, and composition can keep business logic independent of infrastructure.
